questions.question: Which event was contested at the Olympics from 1900 to 1920 but never returned as a regular discipline?

answers.text: Tug of war
Stone lifting
Log throwing

questions.fun_fact: Britain won all three medals at the 1908 Games because teams entered as separate London police units — City Police took gold, Liverpool Police silver, and Metropolitan Police K Division bronze.

questions.question: At which Olympics were live animals shot for medals as an officially contested event?

answers.text: Paris 1900
Athens 1896
St. Louis 1904

questions.fun_fact: Live pigeon shooting featured nearly 300 birds shot from cages. Belgian Leon de Lunden won with 21 kills. It was the only Olympics where animals were intentionally killed for sport.

questions.question: What unusual feat did Eric Moussambani from Equatorial Guinea achieve at the Sydney 2000 Olympics?

answers.text: He won his 100m freestyle heat after both rivals were disqualified — with one of the slowest Olympic times ever
He set a world record despite never training in a 50m pool
He swam the entire race underwater on a single breath

questions.fun_fact: Moussambani had only learned to swim eight months earlier in a 20m hotel pool. He finished in 1:52.72 — slower than most Olympic 200m times — but the crowd of 17,000 gave him a standing ovation.

questions.question: Art competitions — for painting, sculpture, literature, music and architecture — once awarded Olympic medals. When were they last held?

answers.text: London 1948
Berlin 1936
Stockholm 1912

questions.fun_fact: Pierre de Coubertin himself won gold for literature in 1912 under a pseudonym for his poem 'Ode to Sport'. The medals were dropped because most competing artists were professionals, violating amateur rules.

questions.question: Solo synchronised swimming was an Olympic event in 1984, 1988 and 1992. What's odd about its name?

answers.text: A single swimmer was 'synchronising' only with the music
Swimmers competed against their own mirrored reflection
Two athletes performed but only one was scored

questions.fun_fact: Critics mocked the event as the most contradictory in Olympic history. It was dropped after Barcelona 1992 because the IOC added a team event for Atlanta 1996 and chose to keep duet + team rather than carry three sub-disciplines.

questions.question: At the 1904 St. Louis Olympics marathon, the gold medallist nearly died. What had he ingested mid-race?

answers.text: Strychnine mixed with brandy and raw egg whites
Raw opium dissolved in milk
Pure ether on sugar cubes

questions.fun_fact: Thomas Hicks's handlers gave him strychnine — a rat poison that acts as a stimulant in tiny doses — twice during the race. He had to be carried across the line and could not collect his medal in person.

questions.question: Why was the marathon distance fixed at exactly 42.195 km (26 miles 385 yards)?

answers.text: To finish in front of the royal box at the 1908 London Olympics
It was the exact distance from Marathon to Athens in 490 BC
Pierre de Coubertin picked it from a hat at random

questions.fun_fact: The original 1896 marathon was only about 40 km. The 1908 London course was extended so the start was at Windsor Castle and the finish lay before Queen Alexandra's box at White City Stadium. The IAAF fixed it permanently in 1921.

questions.question: Which Olympic event was scored purely on how far a motionless diver drifted underwater after entering the pool?

answers.text: Plunge for distance (no kicking, no swimming, only the dive's momentum counted)
Tandem cycling sprint
Rope climbing for style

questions.fun_fact: At St. Louis 1904, divers leapt in, then floated motionless face-down for 60 seconds. Distance covered by drift was measured. American William Dickey won with 19.05 m. Spectators found it agonisingly dull and it was never repeated.

questions.question: How did the Olympic torch relay originate?

answers.text: It was invented by the Nazi regime for the 1936 Berlin Games
It dates back to the ancient Greek Olympics in Olympia
It started at Athens 1896 as Pierre de Coubertin's idea

questions.fun_fact: Carl Diem designed the relay for Berlin 1936 as propaganda linking the Third Reich to ancient Greece. It was so visually striking that the IOC kept it after the war — the only Nazi-era invention still part of every modern Games.

questions.question: At the 1936 Berlin Olympics, who supposedly handed Jesse Owens his winning long-jump tip in the qualifying round?

answers.text: His German rival Luz Long
American coach Lawson Robertson
Hitler's chauffeur Erich Kempka

questions.fun_fact: Long reportedly advised Owens to take off well before the board to avoid fouling. Owens won gold, Long took silver, and they posed arm-in-arm — a famous photo of friendship across the Nazi regime's racial lines.

questions.question: What do competitors in the annual Cooper's Hill event in Gloucestershire, England, chase down a near-vertical slope?

answers.text: A 3.6 kg wheel of Double Gloucester cheese
A wooden barrel filled with cider
A live greased pig

questions.fun_fact: The cheese reaches over 110 km/h. Winners get to keep the wheel. Broken bones and concussions are so common that ambulances are stationed at the bottom — the race continues anyway.

questions.question: In the sport of Wife Carrying, originating in Finland, what is the traditional prize for the winning couple?

answers.text: The wife's weight in beer
A year's supply of reindeer meat
A wooden sauna shipped to the winner's home

questions.fun_fact: The 'Estonian carry' — wife hanging upside-down on the husband's back with her legs around his neck — was developed for the championships and now dominates because it leaves the carrier's arms free.

questions.question: Chess boxing alternates rounds of chess and boxing. How can a competitor win on the board rather than in the ring?

answers.text: By checkmate or by their opponent running out of chess clock time
Only by forcing a resignation — the clock doesn't apply
By capturing the opponent's queen

questions.fun_fact: Each player has 9 minutes total on the chess clock spread over multiple rounds. After exhausting boxing, players often blunder — heavy breathing and adrenaline ruin board calculation.

questions.question: The longest professional tennis match on record lasted over 11 hours across three days. Where was it played?

answers.text: Wimbledon
US Open
Australian Open

questions.fun_fact: Isner vs Mahut in 2010 ended 70-68 in the fifth set. The scoreboard initially broke because it wasn't programmed for scores that high. Both players received commemorative trophies and Wimbledon later introduced a fifth-set tiebreak rule.

questions.question: What does an 'Iron Man' triathlon involve, in order?

answers.text: 3.86 km swim, 180 km bike, 42.2 km run
5 km swim, 150 km bike, 50 km run
10 km swim, 100 km bike, 40 km run

questions.fun_fact: The format was invented in 1978 during a debate among Hawaiian athletes over who was fittest — swimmers, cyclists or runners. Naval officer John Collins suggested combining all three. Fifteen people started; twelve finished.

questions.question: In the Finnish sport of mobile phone throwing, what category exists alongside 'distance'?

answers.text: Freestyle, judged on aesthetic style of the throw
Accuracy at hitting a phone-shaped target
Maximum number of phones thrown in 60 seconds

questions.fun_fact: The world record for distance is over 110 m. Old Nokias are preferred for their aerodynamics. Organisers say it's a cathartic protest against mobile-phone overuse.

questions.question: Bog snorkelling, an annual race in Wales, has one strict rule about technique. What is it?

answers.text: Competitors may not use conventional swimming strokes — only flipper kicks
Competitors must keep their snorkel above water the entire race
Competitors must swim with their eyes closed

questions.fun_fact: Racers cross 120 yards of murky peat trench twice. The world record is under 1 minute 18 seconds. Wetsuits are optional but strongly advised — the bog water hovers around 10°C.

questions.question: Sepak takraw — popular across Southeast Asia — combines volleyball rules with which forbidden body part rule?

answers.text: Players may not use their hands or arms
Players may not let the ball touch their head
Players must keep one foot on the ground at all times

questions.fun_fact: Played with a woven rattan ball, sepak takraw rewards bicycle kicks across the net from full height. Skilled players spike the ball downward from above the 1.5m net using their feet.

questions.question: Buzkashi, the national sport of Afghanistan, uses what as the 'ball'?

answers.text: A headless goat or calf carcass
A leather sack filled with sand
A wooden cylinder wrapped in sheepskin

questions.fun_fact: Riders on horseback try to drag the 30-50 kg carcass into a scoring circle. Matches can last days. Genghis Khan's cavalry are believed to have played an early form on the Central Asian steppe.

questions.question: Kabaddi, a contact team sport from South Asia, has one peculiar rule about what the attacking 'raider' must do.

answers.text: Continuously chant 'kabaddi' on a single breath while raiding
Carry a small wooden baton at all times
Touch the opposing captain before any other player

questions.fun_fact: If the raider inhales mid-chant, they're out. The sport featured at the 1936 Berlin Olympics as a demonstration event and has been part of the Asian Games since 1990.

questions.question: Which NFL team is the only one publicly owned by its fans rather than a private owner?

answers.text: Green Bay Packers
Pittsburgh Steelers
Cleveland Browns

questions.fun_fact: Over 360,000 shareholders own the Packers. Shares pay no dividend, can't appreciate in value, and can't be resold for profit — yet the team has held six share offerings (1923, 1935, 1950, 1997, 2011, 2021) to fund stadium upgrades.

questions.question: In football (soccer), what was unusual about the rule for goal celebrations until the 1990s in the English league?

answers.text: There was no rule against removing your shirt — bookings for it only began in 2004 worldwide
Goalkeepers were forbidden from celebrating
Players could be fined for shaking the opposing goalkeeper's hand

questions.fun_fact: FIFA introduced the mandatory yellow card for shirt removal in 2004, citing time-wasting and 'unsporting' behaviour. The rule remains controversial — many goalscorers still strip their shirts despite the booking.

questions.question: What did the first FIFA World Cup trophy, the Jules Rimet, suffer in 1966 and 1983?

answers.text: It was stolen twice — recovered once by a dog in 1966, never found after 1983
It was melted down for charity then re-cast in solid bronze
It was struck by lightning during an open-top parade

questions.fun_fact: A dog named Pickles found the trophy under a hedge in South London a week after the 1966 theft. Brazil was given the original permanently after their third win in 1970. It was stolen again from Rio in 1983 and is believed to have been melted down.

questions.question: What is the maximum legal width of an NFL goalpost upright?

answers.text: About 18 feet 6 inches (5.64 m) between uprights
Exactly 12 feet (3.66 m)
Exactly 24 feet (7.32 m), matching football goals

questions.fun_fact: College goalposts are the same width but were 23 feet 4 inches until 1991. NFL kickers complain that even from 60+ yards, the narrow target is psychologically harder than a soccer goal at any distance.

questions.question: Which feature of the modern football was standardised only after the 1970 World Cup?

answers.text: Black-and-white panels (Adidas Telstar) for TV visibility
Synthetic leather replacing real leather
32 panels in any colour scheme

questions.fun_fact: Before the Telstar, balls were plain brown leather, hard to see on black-and-white TV. The 32-panel truncated-icosahedron pattern was designed at Adidas specifically so spectators watching at home could follow the play.

questions.question: How does a 'safety' score points in American football?

answers.text: The defensive team tackles the ball carrier in the offense's own end zone for 2 points
The defence intercepts inside the 5-yard line for 1 point
The defence forces a punt from inside the 10-yard line for 3 points

questions.fun_fact: After conceding a safety, the team must then kick off to the opposition — losing both the points and possession. It's the only score where the defending team also gains the ball.

questions.question: Which footballer holds the record for the fastest red card in a professional match?

answers.text: Lee Todd — sent off after 2 seconds for swearing at the referee
Vinnie Jones — sent off after 5 seconds for a sliding tackle
Pepe — sent off after 8 seconds for headbutting an opponent

questions.fun_fact: Cross Farm Park Celtic player Todd swore loudly after the kickoff whistle startled him in 2000. The referee was within earshot and dismissed him on the spot — before he had even touched the ball.

questions.question: The NFL's 'Heidi Game' in 1968 is remembered for what unusual reason?

answers.text: NBC cut away from the live broadcast to show the film Heidi, missing the entire ending
A snow blizzard during play resembled a scene from Heidi
A goat named Heidi ran onto the field and stopped play

questions.fun_fact: With 65 seconds left and the Jets leading the Raiders, NBC switched to Heidi on schedule. The Raiders scored twice in nine seconds to win 43-32. Viewer outrage led to the 'Heidi Rule' guaranteeing all NFL games are shown to their conclusion.

questions.question: What did the inventor of basketball, James Naismith, use as the first 'baskets' in 1891?

answers.text: Peach baskets nailed to a balcony
Empty barrels set on the floor
Old bicycle wheels with netting attached

questions.fun_fact: Each made basket required someone to climb a ladder and retrieve the ball — they hadn't thought to cut the bottoms out. The bottomless metal hoop arrived in 1906.

questions.question: The Frisbee is named after which real-world object?

answers.text: Pie tins from the Frisbie Pie Company of Connecticut
A Yale dormitory called Frisbee Hall
An Alpine bird called the Frisbean that hovers in updrafts

questions.fun_fact: Yale students tossed empty Frisbie pie tins for fun. Wham-O bought the plastic design in 1957 from a man who had been selling them as 'Pluto Platters', and renamed them Frisbees to match the campus slang.

questions.question: Where were the ancient Olympic Games held continuously for nearly 1,200 years?

answers.text: Olympia, a sanctuary in the western Peloponnese
Mount Olympus in northern Greece
Athens, in the Panathenaic Stadium

questions.fun_fact: The ancient Games ran from 776 BC until they were banned by the Christian emperor Theodosius I in 393 AD. Athletes competed naked, women were banned as spectators, and a sacred truce halted wars across Greece.

questions.question: Volleyball was invented in 1895 as a calmer alternative to which sport for older businessmen?

answers.text: Basketball
Tennis
Handball

questions.fun_fact: YMCA director William G. Morgan invented 'mintonette' so his middle-aged members didn't have to do basketball's physical contact. A spectator suggested 'volleyball' after watching players volley the ball back and forth.

questions.question: The oldest sporting trophy still awarded was first contested in 1851. What is it?

answers.text: The America's Cup (sailing)
The Ashes urn (cricket)
The Stanley Cup (ice hockey)

questions.fun_fact: The schooner America won the trophy off the Isle of Wight in 1851, beating 15 British yachts. The New York Yacht Club held it for 132 years — the longest winning streak in sport — until Australia II broke it in 1983.

questions.question: Modern boxing gloves were popularised because of which rule reform?

answers.text: The Marquess of Queensberry rules of 1867
The Tunney–Dempsey reforms of 1927
The Olympic amateur code of 1904

questions.fun_fact: Bare-knuckle prizefights of the 1800s could last over 75 rounds. The Queensberry rules introduced gloves, three-minute rounds and the 10-second knockout count — turning boxing from spectacle into a regulated sport.

questions.question: Why are the holes in a golf ball — the dimples — there at all?

answers.text: They reduce drag by triggering turbulent airflow, letting the ball fly further than a smooth one
They reduce the ball's weight so swing speeds can be higher
They were originally just decoration and were never proven to help

questions.fun_fact: Early players noticed scuffed old balls flew further than new smooth ones. Engineer William Taylor patented the dimple pattern in 1905. A typical dimpled ball travels roughly twice as far as a smooth one of the same weight.

questions.question: Tennis terminology — 'love' for zero — most likely derives from which root?

answers.text: The French 'l'oeuf' (the egg), because zero looks like an egg
The Old English 'lof' meaning praise
Cricket slang from the 1800s

questions.fun_fact: The 'egg' for nought theory parallels American baseball's 'goose egg' for zero. Some etymologists prefer 'playing for love' (playing for nothing), but the French connection is broadly accepted as the strongest match.

questions.question: Why does a standard ten-pin bowling lane have exactly 10 pins?

answers.text: To circumvent a 19th-century Connecticut law banning nine-pin bowling
It matches the number of digits on a player's hands
It was a marketing change to lift declining pub bowling revenue

questions.fun_fact: Connecticut banned nine-pin in 1841 because it was associated with gambling. Players added a tenth pin and rearranged them in a triangle — technically a different game, legally distinct, and the modern format stuck nationwide.

questions.question: The Tour de France's iconic yellow leader's jersey is yellow because of what?

answers.text: The newspaper L'Auto that organised it was printed on yellow paper
Yellow was the easiest colour for spectators to see at speed
The first leader insisted on his favourite colour

questions.fun_fact: The maillot jaune was introduced in 1919 to make the race leader visible in the peloton. L'Auto used yellow paper to stand out from its main rival, Le Vélo, which was green.

questions.question: Bo Jackson was a star in which two professional sports simultaneously?

answers.text: MLB baseball and NFL American football
NBA basketball and MLB baseball
NFL football and NHL ice hockey

questions.fun_fact: Jackson is the only athlete named an All-Star in both MLB and the NFL. A hip injury in a 1991 playoff game effectively ended both careers — he later played one more MLB season with a prosthetic hip.

questions.question: How long is a regulation Olympic swimming pool?

answers.text: 50 metres
100 metres
25 metres

questions.fun_fact: Short-course world records (25 m pools) are typically faster than long-course (50 m) records because each push-off the wall gives a brief speed boost. Many swimmers consider 25 m pools 'cheating fast'.

questions.question: What is the highest break possible in a single frame of snooker, under standard rules?
questions.fun_fact: The 147 'maximum' is the famous benchmark, but a free ball at the start can theoretically push it to 155. It has happened once in professional play: Jamie Burnett scored 148 in 2004.

questions.question: How many dimples does a standard regulation golf ball typically have?

answers.text: Between 300 and 500
Exactly 1,000
Around 50

questions.fun_fact: Most balls have 336 to 392 dimples in a precise geometric pattern. The exact number affects spin and flight; manufacturers fiercely guard their dimple geometries as trade secrets.

questions.question: Usain Bolt's 100m world record of 9.58 seconds was set in 2009. What was unusual about his reaction time at the start?

answers.text: It was 0.146 s — slower than several rivals he beat
It was the fastest ever recorded at 0.099 s
Officials initially disqualified him for a false start

questions.fun_fact: Bolt's top speed in that race reached over 44.7 km/h. His relatively slow starts and astonishing top-end were both due to his height (1.95 m) — taller frames take longer to accelerate but cover more ground per stride.

questions.question: What does a baseball umpire signal by sweeping both arms outward at waist level?

answers.text: Safe
Strike
Foul ball

questions.fun_fact: Hand signals were introduced in the late 19th century to help deaf player William Hoy follow the calls. They became permanent because they helped distant fans and players hear-impaired by stadium crowds.

questions.question: Why is a cricket Test match called a 'Test'?

answers.text: Because it tests the players' skill and stamina over five days
After a 19th-century cricket bat factory called Test Brothers
Because the first match was played on a ground named Test Field

questions.fun_fact: Test cricket began in 1877 between Australia and England. With sessions of about 6 hours daily for up to 5 days, a single match can run over 30 hours of play — the longest format in mainstream sport.

questions.question: The standard height of a basketball hoop has been 10 feet (3.05 m) since the sport was invented. Why?

answers.text: It's simply the height of the gymnasium balcony where Naismith first nailed up the peach baskets
It was set at the average reach of a tall man plus 50%
It was chosen at the 1936 Olympics as half the average court length

questions.fun_fact: Naismith nailed the baskets to the running track balcony in his Springfield, Massachusetts gymnasium. The balcony was 10 feet high. Despite players now averaging much taller than in 1891, the rim height has never been raised.

questions.question: Which rule did Formula 1 introduce in 2014 that often confused fans during a race?

answers.text: Double points awarded for the final race of the season
Mandatory pit stops every 15 laps
A reverse grid for the second race of a double-header

questions.fun_fact: The double-points rule was designed to keep championship suspense alive, but Lewis Hamilton clinched the 2014 title in Abu Dhabi anyway. The rule was so widely mocked that it was scrapped after just one season.

questions.question: What changed in figure skating scoring after the 2002 Salt Lake City judging scandal?

answers.text: The 6.0 system was scrapped for a cumulative points-based score with no maximum
Judges were forbidden from talking to each other during competition
Pairs skating was split into separate male and female events

questions.fun_fact: After a French judge admitted to a vote-swapping deal, the ISU replaced the iconic '6.0' system with a Code of Points where each element gets a base value plus 'grade of execution'. Theoretical maximums now run into the 300s for free skates.
